paragraphs.text: This note reconstructs the winter temperature of the upper basin from a single varved sediment core, and asks what the record says about the severity of the Little Ice Age winters there.
The winter of 1542 stands as the coldest on record for the basin, with a mean temperature reconstructed well below the series' long-run average.
The core was recovered from the deepest basin at 112 m water depth, and the varve chronology reaches back to the year 1487 with an estimated uncertainty of two years.
Sediment accumulation rates were estimated from varve counting, cross-checked against two independent radiometric dates at 41 cm and 88 cm depth.
The varve thickness series was converted to temperature using the calibration of Lindgren et al., and the resulting anomaly series is shown in figure 2.
Two intervals dominate the record: a prolonged cold phase in the mid-sixteenth century, and a second, shorter minimum around 1690.
Figure 2 shows the reconstructed winter temperature anomaly across the full 1500–1900 window.
The 1542 minimum is 2.1 standard deviations below the series mean, and no other single winter in the record approaches it.
The reconstruction is robust to the choice of calibration, and the temperature record it yields is stable across the plausible range of the accumulation model.
We conclude that the sediment record preserves a clear signal of the exceptional winter of 1542, and that varved lake sediments resolve single winters where documentary sources alone do not.
